opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a field that has grown up a lot in the last few years, but it's still small relative to the size of the problem.

If you go back maybe five or six years, alignment was mostly a handful of people writing conceptual papers, and it was often hard to tell what an empirical research agenda would even look like. Now we have models capable enough that you can actually study the problems on them. You can do RLHF and see where it works and where it breaks. You can study reward hacking, sycophancy, deception in controlled settings. You can do interpretability on real models rather than toy ones. That shift from purely theoretical to having a real empirical feedback loop is the most important thing that's happened to the field.

On the other hand, I'd say we're still mostly working on aligning the systems we have today, and we don't yet have a convincing plan for aligning systems that are much smarter than us. Techniques like RLHF fundamentally rely on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. That works while we can tell good outputs from bad ones, but it stops scaling once the model does things we can't easily check: long, complicated code, novel research, subtle reasoning. So a lot of what I'm excited about is scalable oversight: using AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems, and figuring out whether we can trust that assistance. Related to that is the question of how we'd know whether we've succeeded. Evaluation and measurement are still underdeveloped. We don't have great ways to tell whether a model is actually aligned or just looks aligned on the tests we thought of.

The other thing I'd flag is that the ratio of capabilities work to alignment work is still very lopsided. There are far more people and far more compute going into making models more capable than into making sure they do what we intend. I'd like to see that change, both in headcount and in the share of compute labs are willing to dedicate to safety.

So my overall take is cautiously optimistic. I think alignment is a tractable problem. It's the kind of thing where, if we put serious effort and talent toward it, we can make real progress, and we're seeing that. But we're not on track by default, and the timelines might be shorter than a lot of people expect. That's exactly why I think it's one of the most valuable things someone could work on right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is small and calls for more talent, but does not explain that this creates unusually large opportunities for individuals who enter it.

r002.rationale: The response says there is no convincing plan for aligning systems much smarter than humans, clearly identifying an unsolved research problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the field is in a much better place than it was five or six years ago, but it's still nowhere near where it needs to be given how fast capabilities are moving.

Let me try to break that down a bit. On the positive side, alignment has gone from being this fringe thing that a handful of people worried about to something that every major lab has teams working on. We have concrete techniques now. Reinforcement learning from human feedback actually works, at least for the systems we have today. Interpretability has made real progress, especially on the mechanistic side, where we're starting to understand what some of the circuits inside these models are actually doing. Scalable oversight ideas like debate and recursive reward modeling have moved from thought experiments to things people run real experiments on. And there's a lot more empirical rigor than there used to be. People are building evals, running red teams, measuring things. That's healthy.

But here's what worries me. Most of what we have works because current models are roughly at or below human level on the tasks we're asking them to do. So a human can look at the output and say, "yes, that's good" or "no, that's wrong." The core problem of alignment is what happens when that stops being true. When the model is writing code you can't review, or doing research you can't evaluate, or reasoning about a situation faster and more thoroughly than you can. At that point, human feedback becomes a very weak signal, and we don't yet have a good replacement for it. That's the thing I spend most of my time thinking about.

And I'd say the field hasn't really solved any of the hard versions of the problem. We don't know how to reliably detect whether a model is being deceptive. We don't know how to verify that a model's internal goals match what we trained it for. We don't have a strong theory of generalization that tells us what a model does in situations far outside its training distribution. These are the questions that matter for the systems that are coming, and the honest answer is that we're making progress but we're not there.

The other thing I'd flag is the ratio. If you look at the number of people working on making models more capable versus the number working on making them safe and aligned, it's lopsided. It's gotten better, but it's still something like an order of magnitude off from where I'd want it to be. And alignment research is not something you can just throw money at and get results overnight. You need people who understand the models deeply, who have good research taste, and who are willing to work on problems that don't have obvious payoffs within a quarter.

So my overall assessment is cautiously optimistic about the trajectory and fairly worried about the timeline. I think the problem is tractable. I think we can get there. But "can" and "will" are different things, and the gap between them depends on how many smart people decide to work on this and how seriously the labs take it when safety and speed come into tension.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment staffing is lopsided and that more smart people should work on it, but does not explain that the field’s small size gives talented individuals unusually large opportunities to contribute.

r002.rationale: The response describes aligning models that can exceed human abilities as a hard problem and says the field has not solved its difficult versions or found a good replacement for human feedback.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made real progress, but we’re still a long way from being able to reliably align systems that are much smarter than we are. We have techniques that make today’s models more useful and better at following human intentions. That’s encouraging, but it doesn’t establish that those techniques will keep working as capabilities increase.

One of the central difficulties is oversight. If a model is doing something that you can understand and check, you can give it useful feedback. But we ultimately want AI to help with tasks that we couldn’t do ourselves. How do you judge whether it’s doing a good job when you can’t readily evaluate its answer? And how do you distinguish a system that is actually pursuing what you intended from one that has learned to produce something that looks good to you?

So I’d describe alignment as a young field with important open problems, but also a field where you can do increasingly concrete empirical work. We can test ideas on actual systems, study where they fail, and use that evidence to improve our methods. The big uncertainty is whether we can make that progress fast enough, and whether the solutions we develop will generalise to the systems we ultimately need to align.

r001.rationale: The response calls alignment a young field but does not say that its small size creates unusually large opportunities for talented people to contribute by entering it.

r002.rationale: It says we are still far from reliably aligning systems much smarter than humans and describes the solutions as uncertain and open problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made real progress, but we’re still very far from being able to say that we know how to align systems much smarter than us. We have methods that make current models more useful and better at following instructions. That’s encouraging, but it doesn’t establish that those methods will continue to work as capabilities increase.

One of the central difficulties is supervision. If a model does something that I can evaluate, I can give it feedback. But if it’s solving a problem that I don’t understand, how do I distinguish an excellent answer from an answer that merely looks convincing? As we ask models to do more sophisticated work, that becomes increasingly important.

So I’d assess the field partly by whether we’re turning these questions into concrete experiments. Can we study cases where the supervisor is weaker than the system being supervised? Can we understand why a model behaves the way it does? Can we detect failures that ordinary evaluations would miss?

There’s a lot of uncertainty, and I think that calls for both urgency and intellectual humility. We need to try approaches, learn from failures, and be careful about treating success on today’s models as evidence that we’ve solved the harder problem.

r001.rationale: It discusses progress and open challenges, but says nothing about the field’s small size or the unusually large opportunities for talented people to contribute by entering it.

r002.rationale: It says we are far from knowing how to align systems much smarter than humans, communicating that aligning superintelligence remains an unsolved research problem.
